newsitem.title: USA: California panel to hear testimony on bullet train.
newsitem.headline: California panel to hear testimony on bullet train.

text.p: A California state commission on Tuesday will hold its first public hearing on a multi-billion dollar proposal to build a high-speed rail system between San Francisco and Los Angeles.

Cost estimates for the so-called bullet train range from $11.9 billion to $16.8 billion, depending on the technology that would be used. Extensions to San Diego, Sacramento and San Jose could push the cost up to $25.8 billion.
To pay for the massive project, bonds would likely be sold, backed by either gasoline or sales taxes or a combination of the two, commission officials said.
The Intercity High Speed Rail Commission has been reviewing bullet train proposals and funding options.
By late December, the commission was expected to issue a final report to the state Legislature and Gov. Pete Wilson about whether a bullet train would be feasible in California.
In a draft report issued earlier this year, the commission concluded that a high-speed rail system was feasible and would boost the California economy.
The commission plans to hold a public hearing on the proposal in San Francisco on Tuesday. In the coming weeks, public hearings in Los Angeles and Fresno will also be held.
If approved by the state, the train could start operating as early as 2005.

Under the high-speed rail plan being considered, commuters could travel the 412 miles from San Francisco to Los Angeles at a maximum speed of 220 miles per hour. The trip would take two hours and 45 minutes.
"We're expecting feedback (at Tuesday's public hearing) from both the general public and public officials," said Daniel Leavitt, the commission's executive director.
